metadata.name: FromSpecs
metadata.description: Flow diagram > Drawn from the specs, checked against the flow tests. The screen-transition diagram since jsonui-cli 1.8.66: drawn from one source — each screen spec's `transitions[].destination`, plus `test.appOwnedScreens[].transitions` for a screen with no spec — with the flow tests checked against it rather than drawn from. Eight sections: why one source replaced two (a declaration with no reader), the closed vocabulary of destination kinds (screen / route / external / none / back / unknown) and what each draws, the resolution pipeline from prose to a screen id (case and separators, depth-counted parentheticals, splitting on or / slash / 、, aliases, multiple screens, parent and sub specs, `when`-gated siblings), the two declaration points in jui.config.json (`spec.transitionAliases` with a refused wrong position, `test.appOwnedScreens[].transitions`) and why aliases are per face, what the check accepts (forward edges and the return edge derived from `back`; back steps exempt; the three reasons; exit 1 after every page is written, outside `--allow-partial`), what is listed without being an error (unresolved as absent, inferred `none` at INFO, no spec directory as one warning, per-face counts), how to read the page (the All tab, groups, the ungrouped bucket, the `warnings N` closing line), and what the mechanism does not give. ~9-min read.

uiVariables.name: nextReadLinks
uiVariables.description: Three closing cards: testing (the files the check reads), screen identity (where a screen id comes from), navigation (how transitions are meant to be written).

notes: 2026-09-10 - Page created on the release that changed the rule, jsonui-cli 1.8.66, as the first article of a new top-level section. Every claim is taken from the library's own canon (`shared/core/screen_identity.json`, `diagram` section) and from the upstream release record, with the reporting projects' names, screen names and per-project counts left out; the four unresolved rates quoted in section 6 are the canon's own figures. Three things on the page were checked against the shipped 1.8.66 tree rather than transcribed: the kind the classifier assigns to each example destination, the field names of an `appOwnedScreens` object entry, and the format of the `ERROR [doc-diagram]:` line and the closing `warnings N` line. This site does not run `generate html` or `generate mermaid` itself, so the exit-1 behaviour is stated from the canon's `flowTestCheck.severity` and the upstream acceptance, not from a run here — the site's own gates regenerate spec and component documents only.

2026-09-10 - Updated for jsonui-cli 1.8.67, which changed three things this page describes. Section 3 gains the id-collision paragraph: two raw ids that normalize alike are one screen to the classifier, the winner is now decided by provenance (layout id, then an app-owned declaration, then a spec's file name) instead of by iteration order, and the pair is named in a WARNING. Section 7 gains the screen spec's own `metadata.group` as a group source, with the order test > spec > app-owned, the `sg_` namespace on the All tab's subgraph ids, and the two clauses the closing line can now carry. What was RUN against the shipped 1.8.67 tree rather than transcribed: the collision WARNING, in both of its shapes (the site run prefixes the owner and advises a rename; `generate mermaid` prints the short form) - a first draft would have shown the site's wording for the standalone command; that a `metadata.group` list puts one screen in EVERY tab it names; the `sg_` prefix and the relative `Back to Index` link, read out of the generated HTML; and both closing-line clauses, the structural one from a run that writes outside -o and the gate-expression one from a run whose shared document slot echoed two token-bearing test names - the line quoted in section 7 is that run's, unedited. What was READ rather than run: the precedence between the three group sources, which comes from the generator's own source and its test suite (10 of those tests were executed here and pass at 1.8.67), and the count of faces whose All tab could not be drawn before the `sg_` change, which is upstream's and is not repeated on the page.

2026-09-11 - Updated for jsonui-cli 1.8.69, which adds `click targets N of M node(s) the graph drew` and `document links N declared, M rebased` to the per-owner diagram line. Section 7 now lists both among the denominators and says why each names its own: M is the id set the graph drew, so a shrinking denominator cannot flatter the ratio, and the document count prints both halves because a face declaring nothing and a face whose paths were already right both report a zero. Two things were measured rather than taken from the release notice, and both changed what was published. FIRST, the notice said the segments join the CLOSING line; they do not - they join the per-owner diagram line, and neither string appears in the closing-line builder. The closing line quoted here is the one marked as a real run's output, unedited, so the correct action was to leave it alone: the same fixture fired under 1.8.68 and 1.8.69 prints that line byte-identically. The line that needed reshaping was the illustrative one, which carries made-up values by design. SECOND, the notice spelled the segments `click targets: N of M nodes` and `document links: N declared, M rebased`; the shipped tool prints neither colon and says `node(s) the graph drew`. Transcribing the notice would have published a line the tool never emits. The fixture used was chosen before the release landed so that one run would exercise a drawn diagram and both closing-line clauses together - a run with no diagram could not have shown the click count at all, and no line here is spliced from two runs.

2026-09-11 - jsonui-cli 1.8.70 appends `this run` to `generate html`'s closing line, so the line quoted in section 7 as a real run's output stopped being that. It was replaced by RE-FIRING the same fixture under 1.8.70 and pasting the result, not by typing the suffix into the old line - the two happen to be identical apart from the suffix, which was checked programmatically after the fact rather than assumed before it. The illustrative line above it took the suffix as an edit, which is what illustrative values are for. One line in the same block was checked and deliberately left alone: `Component pages: N generated, M failed` printed 0 times in every fixture here, but the generator prints it only when a run has component specs (`success_count > 0 or error_count > 0`), and these fixtures have none. That is a conditional absence, not a stale line, and removing it would have been a correction in the wrong direction.

2026-09-11 - Section 8's vocabulary paragraph named 1.8.66 while the site is pinned to 1.8.70, so the page dated itself to a version it no longer ships against. Re-checked against the PINNED classifier with 12 cases - the five Japanese `none` spellings, English `none` and a full English phrase falling to `unknown`, `External Browser` matching and `external browser` not, a URL, and `back`/`BACK` both classifying as back - 0 mismatches, so the paragraph was still correct and only its provenance was stale. The qualifier now names 1.8.70 and says it is the pinned version. Upstream has queued English `none` vocabulary with IGNORECASE for a later tag, which will make the first half of this paragraph false; the rewrite must then be PER MARKER, because the three will no longer agree about case (`_NONE` insensitive, `_BACK` insensitive, `_EXTERNAL` sensitive) and any single sentence about "markers" would be false for one of them. Worth recording plainly: nothing here can detect that staleness. The gates check flags, invocations and output shapes, not vocabulary claims. What protects this paragraph is the upstream notice and the fact that it dates itself - which makes it honest when it goes stale, not correct.

2026-09-11 - An eighteenth gate, `article-claims`, makes this page's behavioural claims answerable to the library. Upstream framed the problem exactly: the kind vocabulary exists in ONE place in the implementation, and this article is a SECOND copy of it made by hand — second copies diverge. The gate runs 18 classification assertions and 1 normalization assertion, drawn from five published passages, against the PINNED classifier on every deploy: the five kinds in section 2's transitions block, section 8's Japanese-only `none` list in both languages, section 8's case-sensitive `external`, and section 3's id normalization. Every claim carries an ANCHOR — a fragment of the text it backs — so a rewritten paragraph fails loudly instead of leaving the check guarding words nobody publishes; that arm was fired by rewriting the anchor phrase and confirming it reds. The decisive arm was a SIMULATED next release: a copy of the pinned tree with English `none` vocabulary and IGNORECASE, which is what upstream has queued. The gate exits 1 and names both the en and the ja paragraph, with the negative controls holding (`Login none required` and `external browser` stay unknown). So the change that will make this page wrong now stops the deploy that would ship it. Refusals were fired too: an unset JSONUI_CLI_PATH exits 2, a toolchain with no classifier exits 1 — a failure to ask is never an answer. The honest limit is unchanged and worth restating here: the gate checks the claims someone wrote down. A behavioural sentence nobody encoded still rots in silence.

2026-09-11 - Upstream corrected a claim it had circulated to thirteen recipients for seven messages: the new classifier reaches an installed face at the next BOOTSTRAP, not at the next tag. Verified here rather than taken on report - `installer/bootstrap.sh` runs `git fetch origin; git reset --hard origin/main` and clones with `--depth 1` and no `--branch`, and there is no ref path in the file at all. This site is unaffected either way: it syncs from the pinned checkout and has no bootstrap mouth, so its reach stays 0 until the pin moves. What it changes is a sentence for READERS. Section 8 names the classifier version it was checked against, which tells a reader when to distrust it - but a reader whose install tracks `main` may already be running newer behaviour than the version named. The site already documents the mechanism (learn_installation.update_note: refreshed with `git fetch + reset --hard origin/main`), framed as losing local edits rather than as running ahead of the docs, so the paragraph now says the consequence directly. Terminology, corrected: the simulated arm of the article-claims gate was described as 'a simulated next release'. The trigger for THIS face is not a tag but the moment the pin moves, so it is more precisely a simulation of the tree this site will next pin to.

2026-09-11 - Section 8's vocabulary paragraph is now written PER VERSION, because the two versions in play disagree and readers are mostly on the one this site does not pin. Measured on both trees the same day: at 1.8.70 (pinned) `_NONE` is case-sensitive and Japanese-only, so `none` and `stays on this screen` are `unknown`; on `main` at 88df835c `_NONE` carries English wording and IGNORECASE, so both read as `none`. `_BACK` ignores case in both; `_EXTERNAL` respects it in both, so `external browser` in lower case matches neither. The consequence gets its own sentence: on `main` the markers no longer agree about case, and any single claim about "markers and case" is false for one of them. There is no v1.8.71 - the newest tag is v1.8.70 and `main`'s VERSION still reads 1.8.70 - but the tag is not what carries this to a reader: an install refreshed by the bootstrap follows `main`, so the newer behaviour is already in most readers' hands. Waiting for a tag before correcting the page would have kept it accurate about the pin and wrong about the audience. The article-claims gate keeps asserting against the PINNED classifier, which is right: the paragraph names the pinned release by number, so moving the pin to a tree with the English vocabulary reds the gate by design and forces the sentence to be rewritten with the pin. The claim labels now say that, so a red reads as "this sentence names a release you no longer ship" rather than as "the library broke". What the gate cannot do is assert the sentences about `main`: it is given one toolchain path, so the `main` half was verified by hand on the date named in the paragraph.

2026-09-11 — the pin moved to v1.8.71 and section 8 was rewritten against the SHIPPED tree rather than against the release notice. `none` now matches English wording as well as Japanese, and the English half ignores case: measured at both pins in one run, `none`, `None`, `NONE`, `stays on this screen`, `no transition`, `in-page`, `tab switch`, `same page` and `switches tabs` classify as `none` at 1.8.71 and as `unknown` at 1.8.70. The negative side was measured in the same run and is published beside the positive, because a vocabulary stated without its edge cannot be checked by a reader: `Target screen or tab` carries `tab` and stays `unknown`, `Login none required` carries `none` and stays `unknown`, and `state change` and a bare `stay` match nothing — every English alternative is multi-word or anchored to the whole value, which is what stops an unanchored word from swallowing an `unknown` the report would otherwise name. `external` did not move and is still case-SENSITIVE, so the markers still disagree about case and any single sentence about markers and case is false for one of them. The article-claims gate did its job in both directions: it red on the bump naming three claims, and the rewritten claims table was then fired against the pin being left, where it reds on seven — a table that could not tell the two releases apart would have been passing vacuously. The previous entry's `main` comparison is retired: that day `main` stood one commit ahead of the tag with a test file as the only difference, so the bootstrap warning stays but the agreement is dated rather than stated as a property.
